entries.b: Anniversary and Valentine's Getaway Packages The short answer Anniversary getaways are planned around a date, not just a place. Lock the dates early, especially for Valentine's week and milestone years, decide up front whether it is a surprise, and tell your advisor what the occasion means so the gestures on property fit your relationship rather than a template. Anniversary getaways are the one trip a year where the date is fixed before the destination is, and that changes how I plan them. With a regular vacation you pick a place and find a week that works. With anniversary getaways and Valentine's getaways the week is already chosen for you, often the same week thousands of other couples are chasing, so the real planning is about protecting that date, deciding whether one of you is being surprised, and making the days on property feel like yours rather than a brochure's. I plan a lot of these from our Long Island office, and the couples who are happiest at the end did not necessarily go farther or spend more. They got the timing right, told me what the occasion meant, and let me handle the quiet coordination with the hotel. This page is about that side of anniversary getaways: how far ahead to book for Valentine's and milestone years, what sells out first, how to keep a surprise a surprise, which gestures a resort can really deliver, and what I need to know so the trip fits. You are not buying a reservation from me. You are buying someone who knows what a good version of your trip looks like and how to build it around what matters to you. The other benefits of using a travel agent are quieter: the hours you do not spend comparing, the decisions you do not have to make twice, and the honesty to tell you when the internet is fine on its own. entries.b: Travel Journal Close to Home, Yet a World Away That is especially true now. With the country preparing to mark its 250th anniversary in 2026, travel within the U.S. offers a timely way to see familiar places with fresh attention. Historic cities, national parks, coastal towns, mountain resorts, music destinations, food regions, and small communities all tell part of the American story. Some are famous. Some sit just a short flight or drive away. Many are exactly the kind of places travelers keep meaning to visit, but postpone because they seem too close, too simple, or too easy to save for later.This is the year to stop saving them for later.A close-to-home vacation can be practical without being ordinary. It can be a long weekend in Charleston, Santa Fe, Chicago, New Orleans, San Diego, or Boston. It can be a family trip to the national parks, a lake escape in the Midwest, a spa stay in Arizona, a food-focused visit to the Pacific Northwest, or a beach break along the Atlantic, Gulf Coast, or California coast. It can also be something slower, with time to settle into one region instead of packing every day with another airport, hotel, and transfer.That is where working with a travel advisor still matters. Shorter-distance travel can seem simple, but the right planning can make it better. Advisors can help match travelers with the right hotel, recommend neighborhoods that fit the trip, build in tours or activities that add context, and make sure the getaway has enough structure without becoming overplanned.Traveling close to home can also make room for different kinds of travelers. Families may want less time in transit and more time together. Couples may want a refined resort stay without a long-haul flight. Friends may want a city weekend built around restaurants, concerts, museums, or sports. Multigenerational groups may prefer destinations with easy arrivals, varied activities, and enough variety for everyone to enjoy the trip their own way. It also keeps travel accessible for those who want value, flexibility, and a vacation that fits real calendars, real budgets, and real life.The U.S. is too big and varied to treat as a backup plan. Its best travel experiences do not always require a passport, a complicated schedule, or weeks away. Sometimes the right vacation is closer than expected, and still takes you a world away from the ordinary.See you at the airport! It’s a historic first for any national cuisine.The designation covers more than a set of recipes. entries.t: Echoes of the Vikings: Exploring Norse Heritage in Northern Europe
entries.d: Oceania Cruises has been sailing the world for nearly a quarter century, but the Vikings got a much earlier start....
entries.b: Travel Journal Echoes of the Vikings: Exploring Norse Heritage in Northern Europe Oceania Cruises has been sailing the world for nearly a quarter century, but the Vikings got a much earlier start. Their seafaring explorations—and conquests—began more than 1,200 years ago. Long before our ships cruised Norway’s fjords or crossed the North Sea, sleek Viking longships cut through these waters, their chieftains barking orders in Old Norse above the wind and waves.A lot has changed since then. Wooden vessels powered by sails and oars have given way to the elegant ships of Oceania Cruises. Grog and grub have been replaced with fine wines and exceptional cuisine. While we visit many of the same Northern European ports once shaped by daring Norsemen, we do so with comforts unimaginable during the Viking Age. From burial ships and reconstructed longhouses to ancient assemblies and hearty Viking fare, these destinations reveal a civilization far more sophisticated than the stereotypes suggest. Norway: Where the Saga BeginsFew places are more closely tied to Viking identity than Norway. In Oslo, remarkably preserved 9th-century burial ships still display their graceful lines, intricate carvings and masterful craftsmanship. Their survival is thanks to an unexpected twist of history: rather than being sent to sea in flaming funerals, these vessels were buried beneath great mounds to accompany powerful leaders into the afterlife.Near Haugesund, Avaldsnes—once the royal seat of King Harald Fairhair—brings Viking life into focus with reconstructed farm buildings and timber halls. Farther north, the Lofotr Viking Museum in the Lofoten Islands features a full-scale chieftain’s hall where blacksmiths forge iron, boats are built and visitors can handle replica Viking tools.Norway’s stave churches offer another remarkable legacy of the era’s transition to Christianity. Built entirely of timber, these fairytale-like structures feature soaring roofs, dragon-headed carvings and intricate details that blend Christian symbolism with unmistakable Viking artistry. Sweden: History with a Side of MeadOn Lake Mälaren near Stockholm, Birka—one of the Viking Age’s earliest trading centers—preserves the remains of a thriving settlement where merchants exchanged furs, silver and glass beads. Nearby, Restaurant Särimner serves Viking-inspired dishes crafted from local ingredients, with specialties such as slow-roasted lamb, grilled trout and roasted root vegetables accompanied, naturally, by mead. England: Where the Map Still Speaks Old NorseThe Viking Age is often said to have begun with the raid on Lindisfarne in 792 CE, and northern England still bears its imprint. Town names ending in “-by,” such as Grimsby and Whitby, derive from the Old Norse word for “farm” or “settlement,” while endings like “-thorpe” and “-thwaite” reflect communities established under Scandinavian rule. The longships may be gone, but the landscape still tells their story. Iceland: Trolls Before the InternetFrom Reykjavík, Thingvellir offers one of the Viking world’s most remarkable historic sites. Here, leaders gathered each summer to debate laws and resolve disputes at the Alþingi, one of the world’s oldest parliamentary assemblies. Standing at the Lögberg, or Law Rock, it’s easy to imagine voices carrying across the dramatic rift valley formed by the slow separation of the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates. entries.b: European Vacation Deals: Where to Actually Save The short answer You save on a Europe trip by shifting timing, not by chasing the lowest listed fare. Travel in shoulder or off-season, bundle flights and hotels into a package, and consider value destinations like Portugal, Central Europe, and off-peak Greece. Ask me for current europe travel package deals and a quote. Real savings on a Europe trip almost never come from a banner that shouts the word cheapest. They come from a few quiet decisions made early, and that is exactly what I help travelers get right. When people ask me about europe travel package deals, what they usually want is more trip for the same money, and the honest path to that is timing, bundling, and choosing destinations that stretch a dollar. Good europe travel package deals are built, not found. The best european vacation deals I book are rarely the ones with the flashiest headline price. They are the ones where the flight, the hotel, and the season all line up, so the total lands lower and the experience lands higher. I want to be plain with you here, because a lot of the market is not. Many of the loudest vacation deals europe listings quietly strip out bags, seats, transfers, or a real location, and the number that looked like the cheapest european vacation packages turns into something else at checkout. My job is the opposite of that. I look for genuine value in europe travel package deals by reading the fine print, comparing bundled fares against separate ones, and steering you toward affordable travel packages to europe that actually hold up. Below is where the savings really live, and how an advisor turns a promising rate into a booked, protected trip. Where the savings actually come from There are only a handful of levers that move the total cost of a European vacation, and once you know them the whole thing gets less mysterious. Most of what makes a trip expensive is decided before you ever pick a hotel: when you go, how you buy the flight and room, where you point the trip, and how you get around once you land. Pull those levers in the right direction and the savings compound. Timing Shoulder and off-season travel is the single biggest lever. Fewer crowds, lower airfare, softer hotel rates. Bundling Flights and hotels bought together as a package often price below the same pieces booked separately. Destination Portugal, Central and Eastern Europe, and off-peak Greece deliver a lot of Europe for less money. Getting around Regional trains and short-haul flights each win in different situations. The cheaper one depends on the route. Shoulder and off-season timing If you can move your dates even a few weeks, you can change your whole budget. Peak summer, roughly late June through August, is when airfare and hotels are at their highest across most of Western Europe. The shoulder seasons, broadly April into early June and September into October, tend to bring milder crowds and noticeably better rates, and the weather in many regions is still excellent. Off-season, the late fall and winter months outside the holidays, is where the deepest discounts live, especially for city breaks. A Rome, Paris, or Lisbon trip in November feels like a different, calmer city, and it usually costs meaningfully less. I help you weigh the trade-off honestly: some coastal and island spots slow down or close in the off-season, so the goal is matching the season to the destination. entries.b: Travel Journal Get More Out Of Your Next Vacation Stretching your hard-earned vacation dollars does not have to mean settling for a lesser trip. In many cases, it simply means making smarter choices early, knowing where value is found, and focusing your spending on the parts of a getaway that matter most to you. A well-planned vacation can deliver better memories, better comfort, and fewer regrets than a trip built around impulse decisions.One of the easiest ways to make your budget go further is to stay flexible. Shifting your departure by even a day or two can sometimes lower airfare or hotel rates in a noticeable way. Traveling just before or after the busiest window can also open up better pricing without taking away the best parts of the season. If your schedule allows, give yourself room to compare dates before locking anything in.It also helps to decide what matters most before you book. Maybe that is a better hotel location, a balcony, easier flights, or one standout dinner. When you know your priorities, it becomes easier to cut the extras that add cost without adding much value. That kind of clarity can help you spend with more intention instead of watching little charges pile up.Another smart move is to look beyond the headline price. A slightly higher room rate may actually save money if it includes breakfast, airport transfers, resort credits, or walkable access to the places you want to visit. The cheapest option is not always the best value. Sometimes paying a little more upfront reduces transportation costs, saves time, and makes the trip run more smoothly.Booking earlier can also work in your favor, especially for popular seasons and destinations. Better availability often means better choices, whether that is flight times, room categories, or promotions tied to early reservations. Waiting too long can leave you picking from what is left instead of what works best.Finally, give your vacation budget some structure. Set aside more for the parts of the trip that will shape your days most, then be more disciplined elsewhere. Splurge where it counts. Save where it does not. That balance often leads to a trip that feels more rewarding, more comfortable, and much more worth the money you spent. And do not overlook the value of expert help. A trusted travel advisor can spot added amenities, better room categories, and booking opportunities that are easy to miss on your own. The goal is not simply to spend less. It is to spend smarter, so your vacation delivers more from the moment you leave home. And the Summer Sizzling Sale is a great way to make your vacation go further, all while saving some money.See you at the airport! entries.b: Travel Journal Beach Chemistry: Mexico Meets The Dominican Republic Whether you’re planning a laid-back island escape, an adventure-filled coastal getaway, or a sun-soaked Caribbean retreat, the right destination – and resort – can make all the difference. From Mexico’s tranquil Isla Mujeres and culturally rich Riviera Maya to the palm-lined beaches of Punta Cana, Dominican Republic, these sought-after locales offer something for every type of traveler. Isla Mujeres/Cancun, MexicoJust eight miles off the coast of Cancun, Isla Mujeres, Mexico is a peaceful Caribbean island known for its laid-back atmosphere, crystal-clear waters, and authentic Mexican charm. Unlike the high-energy nightlife of nearby Cancun, Isla Mujeres offers a slower pace where visitors travel by bike or ATV and enjoy an unspoiled setting ideal for family vacations and multigenerational travel.Located nearby, in Costa Mujeres Cancun, Grand Palladium Select Costa Mujeres is a family-friendly, all-inclusive resort featuring a Baby Club for ages 1 to 3, a Kids Club for ages 4 to 12, and a Teens Club for older children. Families can enjoy three freshwater pools, including a children’s pool connected to a water park, along with popular activities like snorkeling and kayaking. Guests experience true “island time,” with access to nearby Mayan ruins, a 360-degree amphitheater, and the Rafa Nadal Tennis Center. The resort’s Infinite Indulgence® program ensures dining, entertainment, and select activities are included. Riviera Maya, MexicoStretching along Mexico’s Caribbean coastline, Riviera Maya is a top vacation destination known for turquoise waters, world-famous archaeological sites, and outdoor adventure. Popular activities include snorkeling, scuba diving, swimming with dolphins, and visiting nearby landmarks such as Tulum and Chichén Itzá, two of the region’s most iconic Mayan ruins.Grand Palladium Kantenah Resort & Spa is a standout family resort in Riviera Maya, offering a half-mile stretch of white sand beach, more than ten international and Mexican dining options, and colorful rooms inspired by traditional décor. Set within lush indigenous gardens, the resort offers premium accommodations, 24-hour butler service, and a serene atmosphere ideal for relaxation and romance. entries.d: Do you need travel insurance for a cruise trip? A Long Island advisor explains what cruise insurance covers, the unique risks at sea, and what drives cost.
entries.b: Do You Need Travel Insurance for a Cruise? The short answer Travel insurance is not legally required for a cruise, but it is worth serious thought. A cruise moves between ports and countries, medical care at sea is out of pocket, and one missed connection can cost your whole embarkation. A policy can protect the money you paid and the care you may need. Most people book a cruise months ahead, pay in full early, and travel far from home, which is exactly why travel insurance for cruise trip protection comes up so often. Deposits are large, refund windows close early, and the ship sails on a fixed schedule whether or not you make it to the dock. Buying travel insurance for cruise trip situations is really about protecting two things at once: the money you have already committed and your ability to get help if something goes wrong far from home. That is the honest case for travel insurance for cruise trip coverage. It will not make a storm change course or a flight leave on time, but it can reimburse a prepaid fare you had to cancel for a covered reason, help pay for care in a foreign port, and cover an emergency evacuation from a ship at sea. This guide walks through what is cruise insurance, what does travel insurance cover for a cruise, how cruise-line plans compare with third-party policies, and what drives cruise ship insurance cost, so you can decide with clear eyes rather than a sales pitch. This is general information, not a recommendation for any one policy, and you should always confirm the details for your specific sailing. A flight view above the clouds at sunset. Some plans add cruise-specific benefits like missed-port or itinerary-change coverage. The reason a cruise gets its own category is simple. A land vacation usually happens in one place. A cruise strings together several countries in a week, keeps you at sea between them, and depends on you reaching the ship on day one. Each of those facts creates a risk your everyday coverage was never designed to handle. entries.b: What Does a Travel Agent Do? The short answer A travel agent researches, plans, books, and manages trips on your behalf. They handle flights, hotels, transfers, tours, and insurance as one coordinated plan, then stay available if anything changes while you travel. A travel advisor is the same role with a more modern name that reflects the advisory nature of the work. The question of what does a travel agent do comes up a lot, and often from people who are not sure whether travel agents still exist at all. They do. The job looks different than it did thirty years ago — less ticketing, more judgment — but the core of it has not changed. A travel agent uses experience and supplier relationships to plan trips that fit the traveler, then handles the coordination so the traveler does not have to. What is a travel advisor? The same thing, essentially. The shift in language reflects how the work has evolved: travel advisors spend less time booking flights from a terminal and more time understanding what a client actually wants from a trip, then building it. Both terms describe someone who works on your behalf rather than for a booking platform. Below is a clear breakdown of what the job involves, how the money works, whether do travel agencies still exist, and when working with one is genuinely worth your time. What a travel agent actually does, day to day The work breaks into five areas. Some of these happen before every trip. Others only surface when something goes wrong. Research and planning Comparing flights, hotels, cruise ships, tour operators, and itinerary options to find what fits your dates, budget, and the way you like to travel. Booking and coordination Making the reservations, confirming the pieces fit together, and handling the paperwork — all under one reference rather than five separate confirmation emails. Expert guidance Recommending the right resort tier, cabin deck, or travel window based on experience and client feedback, not just a listing page. Travel protection Walking clients through insurance options so the trip is covered for delays, medical issues, or cancellations before anyone leaves home. Support during travel Being reachable if a flight is canceled, a hotel overbooks, or a connection is missed. The advisor already holds every confirmation and knows who to call. Honest advice Telling a client when the trip they described is not a good match for the time of year, the budget, or what they said they actually want — including when the internet is perfectly fine on its own. A travel agent assembles the details so the traveler can focus on the trip. Do travel agents still exist? Yes. Do travel agencies still exist is a fair question given how much has moved online, but the industry has not disappeared — it has shifted. The agents who used to issue airline tickets at a counter have mostly been replaced by booking sites. What has grown is the specialist advisor segment: people who focus on cruises, safaris, honeymoons, group travel, or a specific region, and who earn clients through knowledge and relationships that a checkout page cannot replicate. The trend is toward independent advisors and small agencies rather than large walk-in travel shops. Many work remotely, affiliated with a host agency for access to supplier relationships and booking systems. entries.b: Why Use a Travel Agent? The short answer You use a travel agent to save time, tap insider knowledge, and have someone in your corner when a flight is canceled or a resort disappoints. For simple trips, booking online is fine. For complex, costly, or once-in-a-lifetime travel, an advisor usually earns their place. People ask me why use a travel agent when every airline, hotel, and cruise line is a click away. It is a fair question. If you are booking one nonstop flight and two nights in a familiar city, you probably do not need me. The honest case for why use a travel agent shows up when a trip has moving parts: connecting flights, a multi-island itinerary, a honeymoon you will only take once, or a group that cannot agree on anything. That is where an advisor turns hours of tabs and second-guessing into a plan you can trust. So is a travel agent worth it? For the right trip, yes, and here is the part that surprises people: for many bookings it costs you nothing extra, because advisors are often paid by the travel suppliers rather than by you. The real question is not whether to use one for everything. It is knowing when using a travel agent is worth it and when do-it-yourself is the smarter call. The clearest way to answer why use a travel agent is to look at what one actually gives you. Below I walk through what an advisor genuinely does, where the value is highest, and how the money actually works, so you can decide for your own trip. Insider knowledge Which resort suits couples versus families, which cabin deck is quietest, which connection is too tight. Details a listings page will not tell you. Handles the details Flights, transfers, dining, excursions, and documents lined up so the pieces fit and nothing falls through the cracks. Advocacy when it goes wrong A canceled flight or a bad room becomes one phone call to a real person who already knows your booking, not a hold queue at midnight. Perks on some bookings On certain hotels, cruises, and packages, advisors can add amenities like a resort credit, a room upgrade, or breakfast. Not on everything, and never guaranteed. One point of contact Instead of five confirmation emails from five companies, you have one person who owns the whole trip from quote to return home. A calm flight view above the clouds. The perks point deserves a caveat, because it is where a lot of hype lives. Upgrades and credits depend on the supplier, the rate, and availability. An advisor may have access to them, but no one can promise a specific upgrade on a specific date. When someone guarantees you a suite, be skeptical. What a good advisor promises is that they will ask, and that they know which relationships make it more likely. The short answer An all-inclusive Caribbean vacation bundles your room, meals, drinks, and most activities into one price. A Turks and Caicos all-inclusive suits couples and families who want a calm, upscale beach; Aruba, Punta Cana, and Jamaica each fit different trips. Ask Carol for current options and a quote. The Caribbean is where I spend most of my planning time, and the question I hear most often is where to point a first all-inclusive trip. A Turks and Caicos all-inclusive is a favorite because Grace Bay is calm, clear, and genuinely postcard-worthy, and the island leans upscale and low-key rather than loud. It is a strong pick for honeymooners, anniversaries, and families who want a polished beach without a party scene. That said, a Turks and Caicos all-inclusive is only one path, and the right island depends on how you travel, not on a brochure ranking. My job is to match you to the island and resort that actually fits, then handle the details. Because a true all-inclusive means your room, meals, drinks, and most on-site activities are one price, the differences between resorts come down to atmosphere, dining, and who they are built for. Below I answer the practical questions I get every week, honestly and in plain terms: what all-inclusive really covers, whether a Turks and Caicos all-inclusive is worth it, is Aruba safe, do you need a passport for Puerto Rico, and what makes a Sandals resort a good fit. At most Caribbean resorts your nightly rate covers your room, all meals across the restaurants, snacks, standard drinks, non-motorized water sports, entertainment, and the pools and beach. What varies is the fine print, and that fine print is exactly what I read before I recommend anything. Usually included Room, all meals and buffets, most bars and standard drinks, non-motorized water sports, pools, fitness, and nightly entertainment. Often extra Specialty dining reservations, premium liquor, spa treatments, scuba, excursions off property, and airport transfers on some plans. Worth asking about Adults-only versus family sections, tipping policy, kids club hours, and whether Wi-Fi and room service are truly included. entries.b: SUPERIOR TRAVEL CONSULTANTS · WITH MARY SUSAN SCHILLING Disney Vacation Packages, Planned Around Your Family What a Disney package really includes, how to pick a resort, and why a Disney-savvy advisor saves you time and stress. The short answer A Disney vacation package bundles your Walt Disney World resort stay with theme park tickets, and can add a dining plan and airfare. It is not a resort-style all-inclusive. I build the package around your dates, budget, and the ages of your kids, then handle the reservations for you. Disney family vacation packages are one of the most popular trips our Long Island team plans, and they are also one of the easiest to overcomplicate. The appeal is simple: instead of booking a hotel, buying tickets, and sorting out meals separately, a package pulls the core pieces together so you arrive with a plan. Disney vacations are my specialty at Superior Travel, and I build disney family vacation packages that fit the way your family actually travels, whether that is a first trip with young children or a milestone celebration with grandparents along. Most disney family vacation packages start with a Walt Disney World resort room and theme park tickets, then let you layer in a dining plan and flights. People often search for all inclusive disney packages or disney packages all inclusive, and it helps to know what that phrase means here. At Disney, "all inclusive" is not a beach-resort setup where every meal and drink is covered the moment you arrive. It usually refers to bundling a dining plan with your room and tickets so more of your costs are prepaid. I explain the difference up front so there are no surprises, and I can quote wdw vacation packages and disney resort flight packages once I know your travel window. What a Disney vacation package can bundle Think of a package as a set of building blocks. You do not have to add every one, and the right mix depends on your group and your budget. Here is what typically goes into the packages I plan. Resort stay A room at a Walt Disney World resort hotel, which keeps you close to the parks and inside the on-site transportation network. Theme park tickets Multi-day tickets, with an optional add-on that lets you visit more than one park in a single day. Dining plan Prepaid meals and snacks so more of your food budget is handled before you go. This is the piece people mean by "all inclusive." Airfare Flights can be added to create disney resort flight packages, so your travel and stay are booked together. A quiet flight scene above the clouds. What "all inclusive" really means at Disney This is where a lot of families get tripped up. When you see all inclusive disney packages advertised, it almost always points to a dining plan bundled with your room and tickets, not the drinks-and-buffet model you might picture from a Caribbean resort. A dining plan can prepay a set number of meals and snacks per person, per night, which makes budgeting easier and can be a good value for families who plan to eat table-service meals. It is not automatically the cheapest option for everyone, though. If your kids are light eaters or you plan to grab quick counter-service meals, paying as you go can cost less. I look at how your family actually eats, not just the brochure math. If a dining plan makes sense for your trip, I will say so. If it does not, I will tell you that too. entries.b: SUPERIOR TRAVEL CONSULTANTS · WITH LOIS HOWES Escorted Tours and River Cruises How guided land tours and river sailings work, and how to pick the right one with an advisor. The short answer An escorted tour is a guided, pre-planned trip where a tour manager handles logistics, transport, hotels, and daily sightseeing for a group. A river cruise floats that idea down waterways like the Rhine and Danube. Collette is one well-known operator in this space. Ask me for current dates and a quote. If you like the idea of seeing a lot without planning every detail, an escorted tour may be your style, and Collette is one of the names my clients ask me about most often. entries.b: SUPERIOR TRAVEL CONSULTANTS · WITH JAMES McPARLAND Punta Cana, Antigua and Sandals Resort Guide How to choose the right Caribbean couples escape, island by island and resort by resort. I match you to the right island and property, weigh Punta Cana adults-only all-inclusive alternatives, and get you a current quote. People ask me for the best Sandals resort as if there is one right answer, and my honest reply is that the best Sandals resort is the one that fits how you and your partner actually like to travel. Sandals runs adults-only, couples-only all-inclusive resorts across several Caribbean islands, and each island gives the brand a different personality. The best Sandals resort for a lively, walkable stay is not the same as the best Sandals resort for a quiet, romantic hideaway, so the first question I ask is what you want your days to feel like. That is where an advisor earns their keep. When you tell me you are comparing the best Sandals resort for couples against a Punta Cana adults only all inclusive, or wrestling with antigua vs st lucia and antigua vs barbados, I can line those choices up against your priorities instead of a marketing page. entries.b: SUPERIOR TRAVEL CONSULTANTS · WITH RENATA BOULOS Romantic Getaways and Anniversary Packages A destination and resort guide for couples, any time of year: which regions and property styles fit the way the two of you travel. The short answer The best romantic getaways start with the resort style, not the postcard. Adults-only all-inclusives suit couples who want simplicity, boutique hotels and villas suit privacy, overwater bungalows are a splurge, and a city break suits couples who would rather walk than lounge. I match the region and property to how you travel, then confirm the room category and inclusions before I recommend anything. Most of the couples I work with do not need help choosing a beach. They need help choosing the right kind of place, because romantic getaways succeed or fail on the property and the room, not on the name of the island. I plan romantic getaways year round, and my first questions are the same in February and September: how do the two of you like to spend a day, how far will you fly, and what does privacy mean to you. A couple who wants a quiet pool and a couple who wants a new restaurant nightly should not end up at the same resort. This page is my working guide to those choices: the resort styles that suit couples and who each is for, where each style is strongest, when each destination is at its best, and how I read room categories and inclusions before a property reaches your shortlist. Romantic getaways planned this way feel effortless because the fit was right from the start. If you are planning around a date or a milestone year, my companion page on anniversary and Valentine's getaways covers the occasion side; this one is about choosing the place. Quiet beach seating beside the ocean at sunset. Resort styles for couples, and who each one suits Before we talk about where, I want to know what kind of stay you are picturing, because each style trades something for something else, and the wrong one feels wrong in any setting. Adults-only all-inclusive One price for meals, drinks, and most activities, with no children on property. The simplest way to unplug; Punta Cana, Antigua, and Sandals are where I place many of them. Boutique hotel Fewer rooms, staff who learn your names, often stronger food. For couples who prefer one excellent restaurant to six pools. Overwater bungalow Found mainly in the Maldives, French Polynesia, and a few Caribbean spots. Worth it when the room itself is the destination. Private villa Your own pool, kitchen, and silence. A strong fit for longer stays and couples who want to set their own schedule, often with a private chef. City break Museums, restaurants, and long walks instead of a beach. Europe suits a week; a US city suits a long weekend. Beach plus a second chapter Pair a resort stay with a safari or a few city nights so the trip has one slow part and one memorable part. entries.d: Travel is transformational. It changes your perspective, broadens your mind, frees your spirit, and opens you up to new opportunities and possibilities.
entries.b: Your Superior Travel Consultants advisor MARY SUSAN SCHILLING Travel is transformational. It changes your perspective, broadens your mind, frees your spirit, and opens you up to new opportunities and possibilities. As a Travel Consultant with Superior Travel Consultants, I specialize in cruises, all-inclusive vacations, and curated travel experiences for families, solo travelers, and groups. Cruising is one of my greatest travel passions. There's something special about waking up to a new destination, enjoying everything a ship has to offer, and experiencing multiple places in one unforgettable journey. Whether you're a first-time cruiser or a seasoned traveler looking for your next adventure at sea, I enjoy helping clients find the cruise experience that best fits their travel style. I believe travel can be about much more than simply getting away. Whether you're looking for adventure, relaxation, connection, celebration, or an opportunity to rest and recharge, the right travel experience can create lasting memories and give you a fresh perspective. Some of my favorite destinations include Alaska, Aruba, Bermuda, Ireland, Mexico, and the Caribbean, and I love helping clients discover the experiences that make each destination unique. Personally, I also enjoy exploring different cultures, learning about the history and stories behind the places I visit, and discovering the people, traditions, and experiences that give each destination its own character. With a background in event planning, I'm especially passionate about organizing family reunions, group trips, and memorable getaways that bring people together. I take the time to understand each client's needs, preferences, expectations, and priorities so I can help match them with the destination and experience that's right for them. I'm also passionate about the growing role travel can play in helping people step away from the demands of everyday life to rest, reset, recharge, and reconnect. From relaxing all-inclusive escapes to meaningful group experiences, I believe travel can provide the space we sometimes need to return home feeling refreshed and renewed. Travel has been one of my strongest passions for as long as I can remember, and I love helping others experience the joy, discovery, connection, and transformation that travel can bring.
